clue.text: Lady Mary reportedly quarrelsome in Verona

indicators.note: reportedly signals that the clue words are to be taken as heard, sounded out rather than spelt

parts.note: the feuding house of Romeo in Shakespeare's Verona tragedy, forever brawling with the Capulets

explanation.surface: A remark that some titled lady was a notorious squabbler in the Italian city.
explanation.walkthrough: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu was the eighteenth-century letter-writer; her surname is pronounced like that of Romeo's family, but spelt without the final E.
explanation.definitionFit: Lady Mary Wortley is the famous eighteenth-century letter-writer and traveller who bore this married surname.

clue.text: Like Phyllis Bentley's tragedy or John Galsworthy's comedy

definitions.text: Like Phyllis Bentley's tragedy or John Galsworthy's comedy

parts.words: Like Phyllis Bentley's tragedy or John Galsworthy's comedy
parts.note: Bentley wrote a 1929 novel titled A ___ Tragedy, and Galsworthy's second Forsyte trilogy is A ___ Comedy; one adjective fills both titles

explanation.surface: A literary comparison between two English novelists' works.
explanation.definitionFit: Both book titles use the same adjective meaning up-to-date or of the present day.

clue.text: Horatio Fizkin, Esq, was that of the Buffs

definitions.text: Horatio Fizkin, Esq, was that of the Buffs

parts.words: Horatio Fizkin, Esq, was that of the Buffs
parts.note: in Pickwick Papers, at the Eatanswill election, Fizkin is the parliamentary candidate put forward by the Buff party against the Blues' Slumkey

explanation.surface: A gentleman's connection to a regiment nicknamed the Buffs.
explanation.walkthrough: The Buffs sounds like the old British army regiment, but here it is the Dickensian political faction in Pickwick Papers.
explanation.definitionFit: Fizkin was the candidate proposed by the Buff party, that is, the person they put up for election.

clue.text: Corneille protagonist, a count his disguise

indicators.note: to disguise something is to alter its appearance, so the preceding letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A French tragic hero who is a nobleman going about in disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: A Seleucid prince who is a leading figure in Corneille's tragedy Rodogune.

clue.text: Mrs Bennet identified a truth thus acknowledged

definitions.text: Mrs Bennet identified a truth thus acknowledged

parts.words: Mrs Bennet identified a truth thus acknowledged
parts.note: Pride and Prejudice opens with the truth that a single man of fortune must want a wife, acknowledged by everyone, which Mrs Bennet takes to heart

explanation.surface: A remark about the matchmaking mother in Austen's novel recognising a common truth.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb from Austen's famous first sentence, meaning by everyone everywhere.

clue.text: Playwright said to be turbulent in play

indicators.note: said signals that the clue words are to be heard rather than spelt out

parts.note: Thomas Becket, Henry II's 'turbulent priest', is the title figure of plays by Tennyson and Anouilh

explanation.surface: A dramatist who is reputed to behave wildly while acting on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry II's complaint about 'this turbulent priest' points to the archbishop, who is spelt with one T; the Irish playwright Samuel has two.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel of Waiting for Godot is a famous dramatist with this surname.

clue.text: Recognizable, A. D. Godley tells us, by its smell and hideous hum

definitions.text: Recognizable, A. D. Godley tells us, by its smell and hideous hum

parts.words: Recognizable, A. D. Godley tells us, by its smell and hideous hum
parts.note: Godley's macaronic poem on the motor vehicle runs 'Yes, the smell and hideous hum / Indicat Motorem ...'

explanation.surface: A scholar's description of some noisy, smelly thing.
explanation.definitionFit: Godley's comic Latin-English verses describe a motor omnibus, a public road vehicle.

clue.text: Mr Williams, whose adventures exemplified things as they are

definitions.text: Mr Williams, whose adventures exemplified things as they are

parts.words: Mr Williams, whose adventures exemplified things as they are
parts.note: William Godwin's novel is titled Things as They Are; or, The Adventures of ___ Williams

explanation.surface: A man whose escapades showed the world as it really is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Things as they are' reads as plain speech but is the main title of Godwin's 1794 novel.
explanation.definitionFit: The forename of Godwin's hero, the servant persecuted by Falkland.

clue.text: "And Mary, in that simple dress / —s us more, by studying less" (W. M. Praed)

definitions.text: "And Mary, in that simple dress / —s us more, by studying less" (W. M. Praed)

parts.words: "And Mary, in that simple dress / —s us more, by studying less" (W. M. Praed)
parts.note: a quotation with a missing verb: Mary, dressed simply, captivates her admirers all the more for making less effort

explanation.surface: A couplet praising a girl whose plain dress charms more than finery.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing verb means captivates or holds spellbound, rhyming loosely in sense with the poem's admiration.

clue.text: Spirit of Arnold Bennett

definitions.meaning: a spirit is a spectre or apparition of the dead
Bennett's 1907 novel is a supernatural tale with this title

explanation.surface: The soul or essence of a famous Potteries novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: A phantom is a spirit, and the same phrase is the title of an Arnold Bennett novel.

clue.text: Jonson's poetaster said to be Dekker

definitions.text: Jonson's poetaster said to be Dekker

parts.words: Jonson's poetaster said to be Dekker
parts.note: in Jonson's satire Poetaster, the hack playwright Fannius, a caricature of Thomas Dekker, bears this first name

explanation.surface: A claim that a minor poet mocked by Jonson was really his rival Dekker.
explanation.definitionFit: The character's name in Poetaster, the play-dresser generally taken as Jonson's lampoon of Dekker.

clue.text: Articles in French and English produce forgetfulness

parts.note: le is a French definite article
the is the English definite article, 'Articles' covering both languages

explanation.surface: A claim that the little words of two languages make one forget things.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth, drinking from the underworld river of this name brought oblivion, so the name stands for forgetfulness.

clue.text: Beethoven's, in Op.129, was capricious

parts.note: Op.129 is the piano piece 'alla ingharese quasi un capriccio', popularly Rage over a Lost Penny, a piece in a returning-theme form

explanation.surface: A comment that one of Beethoven's late piano works was whimsical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capricious' looks like a judgement on the music, but it translates the piece's subtitle, a capriccio.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical form with a recurring main theme; Beethoven's Op.129 is one marked a capriccio.

clue.text: Capital review

definitions.meaning: a capital city, here that of Scotland
the Whig quarterly founded in 1802 by Jeffrey and Smith bore this city's name

explanation.surface: A two-word verdict: an excellent critique.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish capital city, and also the famous early nineteenth-century literary periodical named after it.

clue.text: Destroyers receiving 120 years of imperial patronage

definitions.text: Destroyers receiving 120 years of imperial patronage

parts.words: Destroyers receiving 120 years of imperial patronage
parts.note: Byzantine emperors from Leo III in 726 to Theophilus in 842 backed the smashing of religious images

explanation.surface: Warships being sponsored by an empire for over a century.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Destroyers' suggests warships, but these are breakers of holy images, favoured by the Byzantine throne for about 120 years.
explanation.definitionFit: Image-breakers who destroyed religious pictures, supported by Byzantine emperors in the eighth and ninth centuries.

clue.text: Pistol shot, somewhat mysterious, with slender target

definitions.text: Pistol shot, somewhat mysterious, with slender target

parts.words: Pistol shot, somewhat mysterious, with slender target
parts.note: in The Merry Wives of Windsor Ancient Pistol hurls the name of Faustus's devil at Master Slender, an insult whose point is obscure

explanation.surface: A gunshot of uncertain origin aimed at a thin mark.
explanation.walkthrough: Pistol and Slender are Shakespeare characters, not a gun and a narrow target; Pistol's 'shot' is the jibe 'How now, ___!' using Marlowe's spelling of the devil.
explanation.definitionFit: Marlowe's spelling of Faustus's attendant devil, the name Pistol flings at Slender in Merry Wives.

clue.text: Ladies with Great Expectations

parts.note: women who stand to inherit fortunes, with a nod to Dickens's novel

explanation.surface: Women characters in Dickens's novel about Pip.
explanation.walkthrough: Great Expectations points to Dickens, but here it means the prospect of a large inheritance.
explanation.definitionFit: Women due to inherit wealth have great expectations in the old sense of prospects of a legacy.

clue.text: Those who do not believe in Mrs Hemans and Thomas Moore

definitions.text: Those who do not believe in Mrs Hemans and Thomas Moore

parts.words: Those who do not believe in Mrs Hemans and Thomas Moore
parts.note: both Felicia Hemans and Thomas Moore wrote poems with this title in the singular; the plural means doubters

explanation.surface: People who disbelieve in two Romantic-era poets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Believe in' seems to mean doubting the poets themselves, but 'in' means in their works.
explanation.definitionFit: Doubters who refuse to accept beliefs, the subject of poems by Hemans and Moore.

clue.text: Herrick's was to gather rosebuds

parts.note: Herrick's 'To the Virgins, to Make Much of Time', opening 'Gather ye rosebuds while ye may', is advice to young women and appears in Palgrave under a title saying so

explanation.surface: A remark about the poet Herrick's advice to pick flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: The Palgrave title for Herrick's poem, advice offered to young women to marry while young.

clue.text: University banality from Iris Murdoch

definitions.note: the definition names a novel by Murdoch, so the answer is a work from her

parts.note: corn is trite, sentimental material

explanation.surface: Academic platitudes coming from a philosopher-novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Murdoch's 1963 novel bears the name of this mythical horned beast.

clue.text: Fourteenth-century composer in England, in Ireland, and in Italy

indicators.note: the first in says the answer sits inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A medieval musician who performed across England, Ireland and Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across the end of 'England' and 'in I'; the closing 'and in Italy' adds that the blind Florentine organist worked in Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: Francesco, the blind Florentine organist, is the leading Italian Ars Nova composer of the 1300s.

clue.text: Verses for Saturday dances in Germany

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for Saturday
Tänze is German for dances

explanation.surface: Poems composed for weekend dances held in Germany.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian plural of stanza, used in English for groups of lines of poetry.

clue.text: Three of a kind; so not William and Mary?

definitions.meaning: in card games, three cards of the same rank
William and Mary were a royal pair, which is not the same phrase reversed

explanation.surface: A query whether a trio means the joint monarchs do not count.
explanation.walkthrough: William III and Mary II reigned jointly, a royal pair; swap the words and you have the old card term, which means three, not two.
explanation.definitionFit: An old card-game term for a set of three matching cards.

clue.text: A feminine one is polysyllabic

parts.note: in prosody, a feminine ending has a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed one, as in motion/ocean

explanation.surface: A grammatical observation that female words have many syllables.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Feminine' seems to be about gender, but in verse it names a chime of two or more syllables with the stress before the last.
explanation.definitionFit: A correspondence of sounds at line ends; a feminine one spans more than one syllable.

clue.text: Stern sort of painter

indicators.note: sort here is taken as a verb, to rearrange the letters of the word before it

explanation.surface: A severe kind of artist.
explanation.definitionFit: Max, the German Dada and Surrealist artist, bears this surname.

clue.text: Gate director for film

definitions.meaning: in Homer and Virgil false dreams come through the gate of this material
James, of the Merchant team, directed A Room with a View

explanation.surface: A film-maker associated with a gate.
explanation.definitionFit: Dreams pass through gates of horn and of this tusk material, and James of that surname directed films.

clue.text: Douglas's was simply splendid

parts.note: Lloyd C. Douglas's 1929 novel is titled Magnificent ___, and 'splendid' paraphrases its adjective

explanation.surface: Praise for someone named Douglas who was just marvellous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Simply splendid' sounds like praise, but it stands for Magnificent, the first word of Douglas's title.
explanation.definitionFit: A fixation or compulsive preoccupation, the noun in Douglas's title Magnificent ___.

clue.text: Keats wrote one on an old pot

definitions.text: Keats wrote one on an old pot

parts.words: Keats wrote one on an old pot
parts.note: Keats's poem on a Grecian Urn, the urn being an ancient vessel

explanation.surface: A poet scribbling on an ancient piece of crockery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' seems to mean written on the surface of the pot, but it means about it.
explanation.definitionFit: A lyric poem addressed to or about a subject, like Keats's on a Grecian urn.

clue.text: Because religious education is genuine

parts.note: since means because
RE is the abbreviation for religious education, a British school subject

explanation.surface: A claim that faith lessons are authentic.
explanation.definitionFit: Honest and heartfelt, free of pretence, as a genuine apology is.

clue.text: Saint is bringing it back at new English chapel

indicators.note: bringing it back says the little word it is written backwards

parts.note: taken as written before turning

explanation.surface: A saint returns a holy relic to a newly built English chapel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns IT into TI, placed after S and IS.
explanation.definitionFit: The Vatican's papal chapel painted by Michelangelo bears this name.
